claims.text: A budget is a financial plan for a future period, agreed in advance and set out in numbers - money, quantities, or both - for the business as a whole or for one part of it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Measuring performance means comparing what a business actually achieved with a stated yardstick for the same period, so that the actual figure can be judged rather than only recorded.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A budget supplies that yardstick for revenue, individual costs, profit, output or cash, and it names the budget holder - the manager answerable for the difference between plan and outcome. The measurement is fair to that manager to the extent that the figures are ones the manager's own decisions can move, which is what is meant by controllability.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Performance against budget is measured as the actual figure minus the budgeted figure for the same item and the same period, and the same difference divided by the budgeted figure expresses it as a percentage of the plan.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A forecast is a prediction of what is expected to happen; a budget is a plan the business commits to and holds people to. Because a budget is agreed before the period it covers, a comparison against it measures the accuracy of the original assumptions as well as the performance of the manager.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Writing a plan in numbers forces a business to be specific about what it intends, and the arithmetic can expose a problem - a month when payments exceed receipts, or a production target beyond capacity - while there is still time to act on it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A budget co-ordinates departments by committing them to the same set of numbers, so that the volume production plans for is the volume sales expects to sell and the volume the buyer orders materials for.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A budget delegates spending authority within a limit: a manager may commit money up to the budgeted amount without seeking approval for each decision, which speeds decisions up while keeping them inside a total the business has chosen.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A target set in a budget can motivate the people held to it where it is achievable and where they had a say in setting it; a target imposed from above and believed to be out of reach tends to be abandoned rather than pursued.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Budgeting takes management time, which in a small business is time taken from selling, buying or doing the work, and the figures rest on assumptions about prices, demand and costs that may turn out wrong.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Budgetary slack is padding built into a budget - costs overstated or revenue understated - so that the target is comfortable to meet. It makes performance look better than it is and ties up resources another part of the business could have used.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A budget can make a business rigid, where a manager turns down worthwhile spending because it is not in the plan, or spends what is left of an allowance near the year end to protect the following year's figure.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Incremental budgeting sets each figure by taking the previous period's figure and adjusting it by an amount or a percentage for expected changes, such as inflation or a planned change in output.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Incremental budgeting is quick, cheap and suited to stable conditions, but because it starts from what was spent last time it carries that spending forward without re-examining it, so a cost that has stopped serving a purpose can survive for years inside the base.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A flexible budget is one recalculated at the level of output actually achieved: variable items are recomputed at the actual volume, while fixed items stay at the budgeted amount because they do not move with output.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Flexing makes the comparison like for like. Without it, a business that produced more than planned shows variable costs above budget for no reason other than the extra output, and the part of the difference that is about price or usage cannot be seen.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Zero budgeting, also called zero-based budgeting, starts every item at zero for each period and funds it where the manager justifies the spending afresh, so that nothing is carried forward by right.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Zero budgeting suits discretionary spending such as marketing, training and head-office services, and is the direct answer to costs that incremental budgeting has carried forward unexamined. It takes far more management time, and it can reward the manager who argues best rather than the activity worth most.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Budgets allocate resources by dividing a limited total - cash, labour hours, materials - between competing departments before the period begins, so the claims are compared with each other against the business's objectives rather than approved one at a time as they arrive.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Budgetary control is the routine of comparing actual figures with the budget at regular intervals, identifying the differences, investigating the significant ones and acting on what is found.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Monitoring against a budget during the period gives early warning: a cost running above plan in month two leaves ten months in which to correct it, while the same information at the year end reports a result that is already fixed.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Management by exception directs attention to the items that differ materially from plan, using a threshold the business sets for itself, because investigating every small difference costs more management time than it recovers.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A variance is the difference between a budgeted figure and the actual figure for the same item over the same period.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A variance is favourable where the difference leaves profit higher than the budget allowed for - revenue above budget, or a cost below it - and adverse where it leaves profit lower - revenue below budget, or a cost above it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The labels favourable and adverse describe the direction in which a difference pushes profit. They are not a verdict on how well anyone has worked, and they say nothing about the cause.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A favourable variance is not automatically good news: materials bought below budget may be a lower grade that raises waste and customer returns in a later period, and a maintenance cost below budget may be maintenance postponed rather than saved.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An adverse variance is not automatically a fault: overtime paid to complete an unexpectedly large order raises the wage cost above budget at the same time as it raises revenue above budget.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Where actual output differs from planned output, part of any variable cost variance is the volume difference alone, which is why the budget is flexed to the actual output before the remainder is read as a matter of price or usage.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The sales revenue variance is the actual revenue minus the budgeted revenue: a positive result is favourable and a negative one adverse.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A cost variance is the budgeted cost minus the actual cost: a positive result is favourable, because less was spent than planned, and a negative one adverse.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The profit variance is the actual profit minus the budgeted profit, and it equals the revenue variance plus the cost variances, with favourable amounts added and adverse amounts subtracted.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A variance is a money amount and carries the currency; expressing it as a percentage of the budgeted figure adds what the money amount does not say, which is how large the difference is relative to the plan it is measured against.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Interpreting a variance means saying what the difference means for the business and what may have caused it - a price change, a volume change, a change in usage, or a budget set on the wrong assumptions - rather than restating the figure.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The variances worth investigating are those large enough relative to the plan to matter and capable of being influenced by someone in the business; a small difference repeated in the same direction each period also deserves attention, because it accumulates.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A variance shows the size and direction of a difference but not its cause; it is measured against a budget that may itself have been set on the wrong assumptions, it does not say whether the manager could have influenced it, and it arrives only as fast as the reporting allows.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Offsetting variances hide each other: a favourable revenue variance beside an adverse cost variance can leave the profit variance small while both underlying differences are large enough to need attention.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.
